newsitem.title: CHAD: Opposition cries foul in low-key Chad poll.
newsitem.headline: Opposition cries foul in low-key Chad poll.

text.p: Leading Chad opposition candidates alleged serious irregularities in the country's second round of parliamentary elections marked by a low voter turnout on Sunday.
Many voters stayed away from polling stations, apparently because of the belief that President Idris Deby's party, already far ahead in the first round, was assured of victory.
As polls closed on scheduled at 6 p.m. and ballot counting started on the spot at polling stations, two prominent opposition politicians voiced charges of irregularities.
Former prime minister Jean Bawoyeu Alingue accused officials of illegally handing out new voter cards on polling day.
"New voter cards were distributted to certain persons this Sunday morning just before polls opened," Alingue told reporters. He also said several polling stations opened late.
An official of the party of the Rally for Democracy and Progress party said voter lists had been falsified, leading to confusion at several polling stations.
Police said they had arrested a group of people accused of distributing voter cards. No other incidents were reported in the capital or elsewhere.

Polling stations in the 11 constituencies in the capital N'Djamena where reruns were held were largely deserted during polling. Election officials and state radio reported a similar trend in the interior.

"People are discouraged and estimate that victory is practically guaranteed for the ruling party which was overwhelmingly ahead in the first round," one voter told state radio in the southern commercial town of Moundou.
Deby and his supporters need to get at least 26 seats in the runoff to ensure a majority in the new 125-member parliament.
Final results from the January 5 first round released by the appeal court credited Deby's Patriotic Salvation Movement with 37 seats against a total of 20 for various other parties.

The runoff, like the main poll, is widely expected to show massive support for Deby in the capital and the rest of the largely Moslem north. His opponents hold sway in the predominantly Christian or animist south.
Deby, a former guerrilla leader from the Moslem north, seized power in a 1990 French-backed coup after decades of civil war or conflict with Libya.
After repeated electoral delays, he won a multi-party presidential election in July in a runoff against fellow general Wadal Abdelkader Kamougue from the largely Christian south.
Chad, a sprawling former French colony on the fringes of the Sahara desert, previously had a 57-member interim assembly under a 1993 transitional charter.
Election officials said results would be posted at individual polling stations as counting was completed, but experience suggests it could be several days before official results would be out.
